claim: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) along with bonobos (Pan paniscus) represent the closest extant relatives of humans sharing a common ancestor approximately 7–8 million years ago.
source: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) along with bonobos (Pan paniscus) represent the closest extant relatives of humans sharing a common ancestor approximately 7–8 million years ago (Langergraber et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Langergraber et al., 2012, which provides the temporal estimate of the common ancestor.

claim: Chimpanzees have been documented to use and manufacture tools.
source: Experimental and observational studies, in both the field and in captivity, have documented a range of cognitive abilities that are shared with humans such as tool use and manufacturing (Shumaker et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shumaker et al., 2011.

claim: Chimpanzees exhibit symbolic thought.
source: Experimental and observational studies, in both the field and in captivity, have documented a range of cognitive abilities that are shared with humans such as tool use and manufacturing (Shumaker et al., 2011), symbolic thought (de and Frans, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de and Frans, 1996.

claim: Chimpanzees demonstrate mirror self-recognition.
source: Experimental and observational studies, in both the field and in captivity, have documented a range of cognitive abilities that are shared with humans such as tool use and manufacturing (Shumaker et al., 2011), symbolic thought (de and Frans, 1996), mirror self-recognition (Anderson and Gallup, 2015; Hecht et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson and Gallup, 2015 and Hecht et al., 2017.

claim: Chimpanzees possess some basic elements of language.
source: Experimental and observational studies, in both the field and in captivity, have documented a range of cognitive abilities that are shared with humans such as tool use and manufacturing (Shumaker et al., 2011), symbolic thought (de and Frans, 1996), mirror self-recognition (Anderson and Gallup, 2015; Hecht et al., 2017) and some basic elements of language (Savage-Rumbaugh, 1986; Savage-Rumbaugh and Lewin, 1994; Tomasello and Call, 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Savage-Rumbaugh, 1986; Savage-Rumbaugh and Lewin, 1994; and Tomasello and Call, 1997.

claim: Chimpanzees demonstrate conceptual metaphorical mapping.
source: some basic elements of language (Savage-Rumbaugh, 1986; Savage-Rumbaugh and Lewin, 1994; Tomasello and Call, 1997) like conceptual metaphorical mapping (Dahl and Adachi, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dahl and Adachi, 2013.

claim: Chimpanzees and humans share similar neuroanatomical features.
source: This cognitive complexity together with similar neuroanatomical features (Zilles et al., 1989; Rilling and Insel, 1999; Gómez-Robles et al., 2013; Hopkins et al., 2014; Hopkins et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Zilles et al., 1989; Rilling and Insel, 1999; Gómez-Robles et al., 2013; Hopkins et al., 2014; Hopkins et al., 2017.

claim: Chimpanzees and humans share genetic proximity.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Waterson et al., 2005.

claim: The relatively recent divergence between humans and chimpanzees explains the striking similarities in major gyri and sulci.
source: In view of evolutionary neurobiology, the relatively recent divergence between humans and chimpanzees explains the striking similarities in major gyri and sulci, despite profound differences in overall brain size.
evidence: The claim is based on evolutionary reasoning connecting divergence time to neuroanatomical similarity.

claim: Numerous studies using MRI have compared relative brain size, shape, and gyrification in humans and chimpanzees.

evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting MRI comparison studies.

claim: Previous studies of brain aging in chimpanzees have reported minimal indications of atrophy.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Herndon et al., 1999; Sherwood et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Autrey et al., 2014.
